"ABSTRACT:
Direct position determination (DPD) (a.k.a. direct localization) offers enhanced precision over traditional two-step approaches. This technique, however, involves considerable communication overhead for transmitting raw data. Low-bit direct localization methods have recently been introduced to address this issue. In this letter, we present a gridless, one-bit maximum likelihood (ML) approach for the direct localization of an orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) signal source. A recent majorization-minimization (MM) algorithm introduced a surrogate function for the log-likelihood function, which lacks a closed-form optimal solution and requires exhaustive searches at each iteration. Our method improves upon this algorithm by developing a refined surrogate function that yields a closed-form optimal solution, thereby eliminating the need for exhaustive searches. Accordingly, the proposed MM approach can eliminate grid quantization errors (GQE) by eliminating the search process. Simulation results validate the proposed method's efficacy in mitigating GQE and its efficiency in scenarios with densely populated search grids.

IEEE SIGNAL PROCESSING LETTERS, VOL. 31, 2024 3099 Gridless Maximum Likelihood One-Bit Direct Position Determination Pan Li, Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Jianfeng Li, Senior Member, IEEE, Xiaofei Zhang, and Qihui Wu, Fellow, IEEE Abstract—Direct position determination (DPD) (a.k.a. direct localization) offers enhanced precision over traditional two-step approaches. This technique, however, involves considerable communication overhead for transmitting raw data. Low-bit direct localization methods have recently been introduced to address this issue. In this letter, we present a gridless, one-bit maximum likelihood (ML) approach for the direct localization of an orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) signal source. A recent majorization-minimization (MM) algorithm introduced a surrogate function for the log-likelihood function, which lacks a closed-form optimal solution and requires exhaustive searches at each iteration. Our method improves upon this algorithm by developing a refined surrogate function that yields a closed-form optimal solution, thereby eliminating the need for exhaustive searches. Accordingly, the proposed MM approach can eliminate grid quantization errors (GQE) by eliminating the search process. Simulation results validate the proposed method’s efficacy in mitigating GQE and its efficiency in scenarios with densely populated search grids. Index Terms—Direct position determination, majorizationminimization, one-bit quantization, maximum likelihood estimation, localization. I. INTRODUCTION H IGH-PRECISION localization is critical across a spectrum of applications, including the Internet of Things (IoT), autonomous vehicles, and search-and-rescue missions [1], [2], [3]. Conventional localization techniques first estimate intermediate parameters, like time-of-arrival (TOA), prior to determining the position. Yet, this two-step approach overlooks the constraint that all angles or time delay measurements relates to the same emitter location. Digital Object Identifier 10.1109/LSP.2024.3491020 direct position determination (DPD) (a.k.a. direct localization) paradigm is proposed to address this problem [4], [5], [6]. Nevertheless, DPD encounters substantial communication overhead due to the transmission of raw measurements from observers to the fusion center. In light of this, recent investigations have focused on the development of lightweight DPD methods employing low-bit quantization [7], [8]. Weiss and Wornell proposed a one-bit direct localization algorithm for localizing a stationary emitter using omni-directional antenna arrays [9]. Later, [10] introduced a low-bit maximum likelihood (ML) DPD framework for noncoherent multipleinput-multiple-output (MIMO) systems and proposed a timeconsuming ML solver. This solver, which performs convex optimization using numerical methods for nuisance parameter estimation on each grid, requires extensive computation time on standard PCs, often extending beyond practical limits. To alleviate this issue, [11] employs majorization-minimization (MM) for direct localization in orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems. This MM approach eliminates the requirement for grid-by-grid convex optimization. However, minimizing the surrogate function still demands an exhaustive search over the specified grid points, given that a closed-form solution is unavailable. This letter presents an improved version of the MM approach proposed in [11] and derives a better surrogate function for the log-likelihood function that has closed-form solutions at each iteration. Our main contribution lies in being the first to propose a convergent numerical solution in the field of one-bit DPD, where each iteration has a closed-form solution. Our simulation results demonstrate that the proposed MM method has the ability to eliminate the grid quantization error (GQE) originated from the search process. Besides, the proposed MM method is more efficient than [11] when the grids are dense enough. Notations: ‖A‖F is the Frobenius’ norm; (·)R (resp. SIMULATION RESULTS We compare the proposed method (denoted as ML-MM) with the baseline one-bit ML solver (denoted as MM onebit DPD (MO-DPD)) and the CRLB [13]. The backtracking squared iterative method (SQUAREM)1 is used to accelerate the proposed method [14]. We use root mean square error (RMSE) as the evaluation criterion and the formula is RMSE 1 Mc ∑Mc i=1 √ ‖pˆi − p‖2, where pˆi denoted the estimated p at the ith Monte Carlo (MC) trial, and the number of MC trials is 1000. The stopping criterion is ‖pt+1 − pt‖ ≤ 10−4. The source is located at p = [1498.7 3207.4]T [m] and three base stations are located at [0 3000]T [m], [3000 0]T [m], and [0 0]T [m]. The search area is [1400 1600] [m] × [3100 3300] [m] with grid size r. B = 5 MHz. The path attenuations for the three base stations are randomly chosen as  ̃b1 = 0.3226 − 0.6887j, ̃b2 = 0.4409 − 0.4035j, and  ̃b3 = 0.4138 − 0.5091j. In our simulations, we set N = 128 or N = 16. The number of pilot subcarriers in most modern communication protocols is generally small. While in this work we consider a relatively large (possibly impractical) number of pilots (N = 128), we focus on the conceptual ability to develop a localization algorithm for possible future systems, for which this assumption would be reasonable. The SNR is defined as SNR = 10 log10( 1 L ∑L =1 | ̃b |2/σ2). The proposed MM method is initialized using a rough gird search of r = 10 [m] by treating y n as unquantized data [11]. At low SNR levels, there are many local optima, and with poor initial values, both our method and MO-DPD suffer from performance degradation due to local optima. However, this issue has a more significant impact on our method compared to MO-DPD. Each iteration for MODPD involves a grid search, which allows MO-DPD to reach the convergence condition ‖pt+1 − pt‖ ≤ 10−4 more readily.3 In contrast, termination of iterations in our method requires strict adherence to the convergence condition ‖pt+1 − pt‖ ≤ 10−4. The final result obtained by the proposed method is closer to local optima. Consequently, the performance degradation due to local optima impacts our method more significantly than MO-DPD. Under moderate SNRs, the proposed method achieves the CRLB for N = 128 but fails to do so for N = 16. The CRLB is only an approximate lower bound, and nonasymptotic effects hinder its attainment for moderate values of pilots. Subsequently, we examine the impact of varying grid sizes on the performance of the MO-DPD algorithm. We consider a larger area of 400 m × 400 m. Fig. 3 shows the RMSE curves, and Table I presents the relative time (We want to clarify that the time statistics presented include the initialization time). The performance of MO-DPD deteriorates as the grid size increases. At N = 128 and r = 0.2m, the performance of MO-DPD matches that of the proposed algorithm but requires 43.6 times the computation time. The complexities for MO-DPD and the proposed method are O(NsNiLN ) and O(NpLN ), respectively, where Ns and Np are the iteration counts for the two algorithms. Ni is the number of grid points. Since the surrogate function of the proposed method is looser than that of MO-DPD, Np ≥ Ns. With a large number of grid points, the MM algorithm proposed in this letter demonstrates superior stability in both time efficiency and performance. V. CONCLUSION We improve the MM algorithm recently presented in [11].
